content: FYN, also known as proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase Fyn (p59-FYN, Slk, Syn, MGC45350, Gene ID 2534), is an enzyme encoded by the FYN gene in humans. It is a 59-kDa member of the Src family of kinases, which are primarily involved in T-cell and neuronal signaling during development and normal cellular physiology. Disruptions in these signaling pathways are often implicated in the development of various cancers. As a proto-oncogene, FYN encodes proteins that regulate cell growth. Mutations in its DNA sequence can transform it into an oncogene, leading to the production of altered proteins that disrupt normal cell regulation. FYN belongs to the protein-tyrosine kinase oncogene family and encodes a membrane-associated tyrosine kinase involved in the regulation of cell growth. This protein interacts with the p85 subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and binds to Fyn-binding proteins. Alternative splicing of FYN transcripts results in distinct isoforms. FYN was first identified in 1986 as Syn or Slk through probes derived from v-yes and v-fgr. It is a member of the Src family of kinases (SFK), the first proto-oncogene family to be discovered. A common feature of SFKs is their frequent upregulation in cancers. FYN is functionally distinct from other SFK members due to its interactions with focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and paxillin (PXN), which are critical for regulating cell morphology and motility. FYN is a tyrosine-specific phosphotransferase and a member of the Src family of non-receptor tyrosine protein kinases, which also includes Abl, Src, focal adhesion kinase, and Janus kinase. It is located downstream of several cell surface receptors and is commonly associated with neuronal development and T-cell signaling. Upon activation, FYN triggers downstream molecular signals that drive processes essential for cell growth and motility. It is primarily localized to the cytoplasmic leaflet of the plasma membrane, where it phosphorylates tyrosine residues on key target proteins involved in various signaling pathways. Tyrosine phosphorylation by FYN regulates target protein activity and/or creates binding sites for other signaling molecules. FYN also functions as a tumor suppressor. When its normal biology is compromised, altered FYN contributes to the neoplastic transformation of normal cells into cancerous ones, progressing from pre-invasive to invasive stages and ultimately metastasis. Understanding FYN's role in normal biology is critical for comprehending its involvement in cancer, as cancer often arises from dysregulation of these pathways. Identifying the signaling pathways involving FYN is essential for developing pharmacologic agents to mitigate uncontrolled signaling. Tools used to study FYN's role include cells derived from FYN-deficient mice, kinase-inactive dominant-negative FYN mutants (K299M), and pharmacologic inhibitors of Src family kinases, such as PP2. These tools have demonstrated FYN's involvement in Tand B-cell receptor signaling, integrin-mediated signaling, growth factor and cytokine receptor signaling, platelet activation, ion channel function, cell adhesion, axon guidance, fertilization, mitotic entry, and differentiation of natural killer cells, oligodendrocytes, and keratinocytes. FYN interacts with numerous proteins, including ADD2, BCAR1, C-Raf, CBLC, CD36, CD44, CDH1, CHRNA7, CTNND1, CBL, CSF1R, DLG4, dystroglycan, EPHA8, FYB, FASLG, GNB2L1, GRIN2A, ITK, Janus kinase 2, KHDRBS1, Lck, LKB1, nephrin, PAG1, PIK3R2, PRKCQ, PTK2B, PTK2, PTPRT, UNC119, RICS, SH2D1A, SKAP1, Syk, TNK2, TRPC6, tau protein, TrkB, TYK2, TUBA3C, WAS, and ZAP-70. The Src family of kinases, including FYN, is closely associated with cancer progression, particularly in processes such as invasion, tumor progression, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis, and metastasis. FYN's normal role in cellular growth and proliferation can be exploited in cancer progression and metastasis. Overexpression of FYN has been studied in cancers such as prostate cancer, glioblastoma multiforme, squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, pancreatic cancer, chronic myelogenous leukemia, and melanoma. In prostate cancer, FYN overexpression promotes anti-apoptotic activity of Akt, allowing cells to evade normal cell death pathways. In glioblastoma multiforme, Src and FYN act as effectors of oncogenic EGFR signaling, driving tumor invasion and cancer cell survival. FYN's role in cell migration and adhesion enables it to utilize integrin and FAK pathways for cancer growth. Normal integrin functions as a cell surface receptor that interacts with the extracellular matrix to influence cell shape and motility, while FAK is a tyrosine kinase recruited to focal adhesion sites, playing a key role in directed cell movement. Dysregulation of this pathway allows cancer cells to alter shape and motility, increasing the likelihood of invasion and metastasis. Additional pathways under investigation regarding FYN's role in cancer progression include the Rac and Rho family of GTPases, Ras, Erk, and MAPK. As a result, FYN has become a common target for anti-cancer therapeutic research. Inhibition of FYN, like other SFKs, reduces cell growth. Expression of kinase-dead FYN (KD-FYN), a specific competitor of endogenous FYN, has been shown to reduce primary tumor size in mice. Targeting FYN's unique properties, as well as inhibiting FAK and PXN, holds promise for developing effective molecularly targeted combination cancer therapies. FYN inhibitors are also being explored as potential treatments for Alzheimer's disease.
